newsitem.title: FRANCE: Franco-German summit tries to rescue euro.
newsitem.headline: Franco-German summit tries to rescue euro.

text.p: The leaders of France and Germany meet in Poitiers, western France, on Friday to try to keep the European Union on track towards monetary union and the scheduled launch of the euro single currency on January 1, 1999.

The first meeting of German Chancellor Helmut Kohl with the power-sharing duo of French President Jacques Chirac and Prime Minister Lionel Jospin will focus on a formula for altering the rules for the euro which both sides can take back home without apology.

The Jospin government, which took power last week after an upset victory in June 1 elections, stunned Bonn and other European partners by saying it might want to delay, for last-minute changes, a stability pact aimed at assuring fiscal restraint after the introduction of the euro.

Jospin's Socialists pledged during the election campaign to take a new look at the pact, agreed last year in Dublin and set to be ratified at next week's EU summit in Amsterdam, to redirect it towards promoting growth and jobs instead of austerity.
The failure of France's previous centre-right government to keep similar campaign promises was a key reason for its surprise election defeat.

Germany consistently focused on fiscal discipline and price stability in the runup to a single currency, but Kohl's reputation was dented when his government proposed revaluing the central bank's gold reserves to qualify for the euro.
The stability pact will top the agenda at the Poitiers talks, the latest in a regular series of six-monthly meetings between Bonn and Paris, seen as the dual engines in the drive for European unity.

Financial markets and some European capitals have voiced growing fears that the controversy over the stability pact could be a symptom of a deeper malaise undermining the steady march to the euro's launch on January 1, 1999.

Jospin said after talks with European Commission President Jacques Santer on Thursday that progress had been made ahead of the Amsterdam summit towards resolving France's concerns about coordinating economic and employment policy.

"The preoccupations we are expressing do not simply concern France. They concern the whole of Europe," Jospin told reporters. "Therefore I think these concerns have been understood. We are making progress."
Santer said both he and Jospin wanted to make a success of the Amsterdam summit next Monday and Tuesday, adding: "All elements are on the table to reach an agreement."

Bowing to the EU's new leftward tilt following the British and French elections, Germany agreed this week to add a jobs chapter to the revised Maastricht treaty on European integration which is to come up for ratification in Amsterdam.
German officials said they were also considering an extra jobs resolution to be added to the stability pact in an effort to win Jospin's backing.

Any agreement reached in Poitiers will have to win approval from all 15 EU members in Amsterdam. While most EU leaders are likely to agree to cosmetic concessions to win over Paris, they fear Jospin will be seeking something more substantive so that he can later boast that he fulfilled his campaign promise.
